title: The first jhana
hookLine: like bath powder kneaded with water until it is soaked through: joy filling the body (MN 39)

cards: A boy sits in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father is busy with the work of the day. Nobody is watching him. And something happens: his mind goes quiet and bright, and his body fills with a gentle joy.
Years later, after a long stretch of starving himself and pushing his body to its limit, that grown man remembers the afternoon under the tree, and wonders: could that be the way to awakening?

teach.b: The man is the Buddha-to-be, and he tells this story himself, in MN 36. He'd been wary of that kind of pleasure, he says; then he saw he didn't need to fear it, because it had nothing to do with sense pleasures.
Jhana is the Pali word. In Sanskrit it's dhyana, the same word that traveled to China as chan and to Japan as zen. It means meditative absorption.

In MN 39 the Buddha describes the first one: quite secluded from sense pleasures and unwholesome states, a person enters the first jhana, with directed and sustained thought, and with joy and pleasure born of that seclusion.
Then a picture from a world before bars of soap.
A skilled bath attendant pours bath powder into a metal bowl, sprinkles it with water bit by bit, and kneads it into a ball, until the moisture soaks every grain, inside and out, yet doesn't drip.
That's how this joy fills the body. It's physical: it drenches the whole body. It's thorough: no part is left dry.
And there's still a hand at work: thinking is present, directed and sustained, like the attendant's hands working the powder.
The later jhanas let even that settle.
One honest note: teachers today disagree about how deep this state is.
Some describe a rare, total absorption; others a calmer, more accessible steadiness. The texts give pictures, not a depth gauge.

how: Jhana practice is taught especially in Theravada meditation lineages, usually with a teacher and often on retreat; Chan and Zen take their names from the same word, dhyana.

o: a Pali word for wisdom or insight
a chant repeated to calm the mind

games.q: match the pieces of the first jhana.

s: jhana and zen come from the same word
Pali jhana, Sanskrit dhyana, Chinese chan, Japanese zen.
in the first jhana all thinking has stopped
directed and sustained thought are still present; they settle later.
the Buddha remembered something like the first jhana from his childhood
MN 36: under a rose-apple tree, while his father was busy.

games.q: after years of harsh practice, you remember a quiet joy from your childhood. what does the Buddha-to-be decide, in MN 36?
o: that pleasure is dangerous and must be avoided
that this might be the way, and he needn't fear it
that he should go home to his father
games.why: he saw that this joy had nothing to do with sense pleasures, so there was no need to fear it, and he took it as a path.

practice: No need to reach for joy; look for any ease already here, warm hands, shoulders letting go on the out-breath, a soft belly.
Find one small place of ease and see whether it can spread, slowly, like water into powder, and if you find nothing, that's honest too: rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Jhana. Meditative absorption. In the first, joy born of seclusion soaks the whole body, like water kneaded into bath powder.

orig.note: Pali jhāna: meditative absorption; Sanskrit dhyāna (ध्यान), which became Chinese chan and Japanese zen.

carryVoice: Your line: soaked through. Joy that fills the whole body and doesn't drip. That's day three hundred ninety-six.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the bath powder simile)
